newsitem.title: UK: European gas markets to converge post-1998 - report.
newsitem.headline: European gas markets to converge post-1998 - report.

text.p: U.K. and Continental gas markets will converge in both physical and commercial terms from the end of 1998, following the opening of the Interconnector pipeline linking Britain and Belgium, according to a new report published on Wednesday.
In "The Convergence of European Gas Markets", consultants Wood Mackenzie point out several market trends already under way which have started this convergence.

These include an increase of interconnectivity in European markets, leading to greater cross-border trade such as sales from western Europe to eastern Europe; the development of oversupply in the U.K., causing a price collapse and the emergence of a more sophisticated trading environment; the announcement of gas sales totalling 48 billion cubic metres through the Interconnector pipeline from the U.K. to the continent; continuing development of export capacity from Russia, Algeria and Norway into the EU; and progress on the gas liberalisation Directive, which Wood Mackenzie says may lead to a final agreement between member states this year.

In physical terms, the report sees convergence occurring as selected European markets, especially Italy, show a fully contracted future supply position. Germany is the only European country with competing transmission systems, and potential is seen there for future oversupply as the sum of gas contracted by competing players may exceed aggregate demand.

In commercial terms, current gas supply contracts show an average disparity of 30 percent in prices between the U.K. and the rest of Europe. Wood Mackenzie predicts convergence through the evolution of a range of contract terms, including a move away from oil price indexation on the Continent and an end to field depletion contracts in the U.K.
The report anticipates that the development of trading will be limited to specific locations, such as Zeebrugge, where sufficient sellers and buyers exist to support such activity.

And with power markets also opening up, with forecasts for greater use of gas in power generation, the report concludes that "there is a convincing argument for closer linkage between European gas and electricity markets."
